t: Lexicographically Smallest String After Substring Operation
o: One operation decrements every character of one chosen substring ('a' wraps to 'z'). We want the lexicographically smallest result. Decrementing a letter helps unless it is 'a' (which becomes 'z', terrible). So: if the string contains an 'a' not at position 0, decrement the prefix ending just before that 'a' (example "cbabc" → "baabc"). If the string starts with 'a's, we cannot improve them; instead decrement the entire suffix after the leading 'a' block ("acbbc" → "abaab"). If the whole string is 'a's, decrement just the last character ("aa" → "az") since touching earlier 'a's would turn them into 'z's.
k: Never wrap an 'a' to 'z' — it is always lexicographically harmful.
The optimal operation is a single contiguous range: either the prefix before the first 'a', or the whole suffix after the leading 'a'-run, or just the last character if all are 'a'.

a.i: Find the first 'a' at index f. If f > 0, decrement s[0..f-1]. Otherwise skip the leading run of 'a's (ending at index p) and decrement everything from p to the end; if the entire string is 'a', decrement only the last character. Any other choice either wraps an 'a' or leaves improvable characters untouched.
s: Scan to the first index f with s[f] == 'a'.
If no 'a' exists, decrement the whole string.
Else if f > 0, decrement s[0..f-1]; otherwise let p be the end of the leading 'a' run and decrement s[p..n-1], or just the last character if p == n.
a.t: O(n) — a constant number of linear scans
a.sp: O(n) — mutable copy of the string

w: The greedy is provably optimal: the first differing position decides lexicographic order, so improve the earliest possible characters without ever wrapping an 'a'. Common pitfalls: wrapping 'a'→'z' in the middle, or forgetting the all-'a' case. Follow-up: what if multiple operations were allowed (answer unchanged — one range still suffices).
